entries.title: The Whisperer in Darkness
entries.what: The HPLHS's second Lovecraft feature, directed by Sean Branney: folklore professor Albert Wilmarth investigates things seen in flooded Vermont rivers, shot in monochrome Mythoscope with miniatures and stop-motion Mi-Go
entries.why: The same company's follow-up, made by the same people in the same spirit of period pastiche - Branney and Leman produced, David Robertson shot and cut both, Troy Sterling Nies scored both, Matt Foyer and Barry Lynch act in both - though the HPLHS built this one after 'the classic horror films of the 1930s like Dracula, Frankenstein and King Kong' rather than the silent era. Grades higher than it tones: it talks, it explains, and its last reel hands you the spectacle the silent film kept just out of frame.

entries.title: The Testimony of Randolph Carter
entries.what: The HPLHS's first film and Andrew Leman's earliest Lovecraft adaptation: a 53-minute student production of 'The Statement of Randolph Carter', shot on a home VHS deck in the summer of 1987 and indexed by Letterboxd under 1988
entries.why: Literally the same director's first pass at the same problem, eighteen years earlier and with none of the craft yet: the HPLHS store calls it 'one of the oldest known amateur adaptations of a Lovecraft story'. It is the proof that the 2005 film's style came out of decades of fan filmmaking rather than out of nowhere. Tones lower than it grades: video murk is not the same thing as composed monochrome, and here the cheapness is simply cheapness, not yet turned into style.

entries.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
entries.what: Robert Wiene's German Expressionist landmark: a young man's account of a fairground hypnotist and his somnambulist, told in painted-flat sets that lean and taper, and framed by a narrator you eventually cannot trust
entries.why: The objective centre of the period and mode the film is imitating - silent, monochrome, intertitled, its horror staged rather than photographed - and structurally the same trick: a whole story delivered as one man's testimony, with the frame quietly undermining it. Note this is an attribute match, not a documented influence; nobody at the HPLHS ever named it.

entries.title: Nosferatu
entries.what: F. W. Murnau's unlicensed Dracula: an estate agent travels to a Carpathian castle and brings a plague-bearing thing back to his home town, shot largely on real locations with in-camera tricks
entries.why: The other pillar of the silent horror vocabulary the film speaks - shadow used as the monster, a creature glimpsed and withheld, undercranking and stop-tricks standing in for a special-effects budget. Attribute match on period and mode, not a cited influence.

entries.title: Metropolis
entries.what: Fritz Lang's silent science-fiction epic of a stratified future city, built from miniatures, matte work, the Schufftan mirror process and enormous forced-perspective sets
entries.why: The period benchmark for exactly the toolkit The Call of Cthulhu revives: miniatures, forced perspective and in-camera compositing used to put an impossible city on screen. R'lyeh rising is that lineage on a garage budget. Attribute match, not a cited influence.

entries.title: The Lost World
entries.what: Harry O. Hoyt's silent adaptation of Conan Doyle, the first feature to carry a whole story on Willis O'Brien's stop-motion creatures, composited with miniature landscapes and glass shots
entries.why: The direct silent-era ancestor of the articulated Cthulhu puppet and the miniature R'lyeh: it established that a monster animated frame by frame could hold a feature, and it did so with the same painterly, slightly unreal compositing the 2005 film reproduces on purpose. Attribute match on period and technique.

entries.title: Häxan
entries.what: Benjamin Christensen's silent Swedish-Danish part-essay, part-horror film on witchcraft, which opens as an illustrated lecture over woodcuts and documents before dramatising what it has described
entries.why: The closest silent-era match for the film's method as well as its look: a scholarly frame - documents, exhibits, a narrator assembling evidence - that slides into staged horror, with practical monsters and a mixture of the antiquarian and the lurid. Attribute match on period and mode.

entries.title: Die Farbe
entries.what: Huan Vu's German adaptation of 'The Colour Out of Space', shot almost entirely in black and white so the single unearthly colour can be the only thing on screen that has any, made as a no-budget independent feature
entries.why: The nearest living relative: an unpaid, self-organised crew adapting Lovecraft faithfully and at length, choosing monochrome as a formal constraint and letting the horror stay a suggestion, spending its one effect where it counts. Recognisably the same undertaking in another language.

entries.title: Re-Animator
entries.what: Stuart Gordon's adaptation of Lovecraft's serial 'Herbert West-Reanimator': a medical student's glowing reagent, an escalating body count, and a famously unrestrained final act
entries.why: The most consequential Lovecraft feature there is and the reference point every Lovecraft recommendation has to clear, but it is the exact opposite film to sit through: colour, gore, comedy, and a conviction that showing everything is funnier and better than withholding it.

entries.title: Dagon
entries.what: Stuart Gordon's adaptation of 'The Shadow over Innsmouth' (under the title of a different story), in which a shipwrecked couple find a Spanish fishing town given over to a sea god
entries.why: One of the few Lovecraft features that actually commits to the mythos rather than borrowing a title, and the closest thing to a straight Cthulhu-cult story on film before 2005. Wet, loud, rainy digital colour and prosthetic fish-people, so the register is entirely different.

entries.title: Color Out of Space
entries.what: Richard Stanley's version of the same story, with a meteorite landing on a New England alpaca farm and a colour nobody can name working through the water table and the family
entries.why: The best-known modern Lovecraft adaptation and the other pole of how to film him: saturated magenta light, body horror shown in full, a lead performance pitched loud. Same author, same problem of filming the unfilmable, answered by showing rather than by suggesting.

entries.title: The Artist
entries.what: Michel Hazanavicius's silent black-and-white feature about a 1920s star undone by the coming of sound, made with intertitles, Academy ratio and a wall-to-wall orchestral score
entries.why: The most visible modern film made deliberately silent and monochrome, and the obvious benchmark for the decision The Call of Cthulhu made six years earlier. Grades far above its tone: the pastiche is glossy, warm, expensively lit and out to charm, where the target is grimy, dread-driven and proud of its seams.

entries.title: Blancanieves
entries.what: Pablo Berger's silent black-and-white Snow White, relocated to 1920s Andalusia and bullfighting, with intertitles and a flamenco-inflected score
entries.why: Modern silent monochrome used for dread rather than for charm - gothic cruelty, a wicked stepmother shot in hard expressionist light, a fairy tale that ends badly. Of the deliberate modern silents it is the one whose texture a viewer of the target would recognise most immediately.

entries.title: The Resurrected
entries.what: Dan O'Bannon's film of 'The Case of Charles Dexter Ward', structured as a private detective's investigation into a chemist's family history and the things in his farmhouse cellar
entries.why: One of the most faithful Lovecraft features ever made and, like the target, built as a documentary investigation assembled after the fact. Shot as an early-nineties direct-to-video thriller, though, with creature effects delivered rather than implied. Grades well above its tone.

entries.title: From Beyond
entries.what: Stuart Gordon's expansion of a short Lovecraft story into a feature about a resonator that lets its users see the creatures sharing the room with them
entries.why: A central Lovecraft adaptation and a literal treatment of the target's governing idea - that what is really there is next to us and simply not perceived. Gordon's answer is to make it luridly visible in purple light; the target's answer is to keep it off screen - a strong connection scoring nothing on tone.

entries.title: The Dunwich Horror
entries.what: Daniel Haller's AIP adaptation, with Dean Stockwell as Wilbur Whateley after the Necronomicon and the Whateley farmhouse hiding something upstairs
entries.why: One of the handful of studio-era Lovecraft features, and the other major Mythos tale filmed - Yog-Sothoth, the Necronomicon, Miskatonic. Psychedelic late-sixties colour, optical effects and a rock score put it in a wholly different room.

entries.title: The Haunted Palace
entries.what: Roger Corman's Vincent Price vehicle, sold as Poe but adapted from 'The Case of Charles Dexter Ward', complete with Arkham, the Necronomicon and Cthulhu named aloud
entries.why: The first Lovecraft feature of any consequence and the first time the Mythos reached a cinema screen. Its gothic-studio look - fog, candelabra, CinemaScope colour - is the studio opposite of the target's handmade monochrome: grades strong, tones zero.

entries.title: Die, Monster, Die!
entries.what: Daniel Haller's first film, a British-shot adaptation of 'The Colour Out of Space' with Boris Karloff as the patriarch of a blighted estate
entries.why: The earliest feature adaptation of a Lovecraft story proper, and one of the four films on this list attacking the same story from four decades. AIP gothic colour and a radiation-movie ending; the connection is the source, not the experience, so grade and tone part company here.

entries.title: The Curse
entries.what: David Keith's directing debut, a Tennessee-farm transposition of 'The Colour Out of Space' with a meteorite poisoning the well and the crops
entries.why: A genuine adaptation of a core Lovecraft story and the middle term between Die, Monster, Die! and Color Out of Space. Eighties regional horror with practical rot effects and a family melodrama attached - a different register entirely.

entries.title: Castle Freak
entries.what: Stuart Gordon's loose adaptation of 'The Outsider', with an American family inheriting an Italian castle that has something chained in it
entries.why: A third Gordon-Lovecraft feature and one of the few adaptations of Lovecraft's most interior story. Grim, shot-in-Italy direct-to-video horror that puts its monster fully on screen and keeps it there; the grade is real, the tone is not.

entries.title: The Unnamable
entries.what: Jean-Paul Ouellette's adaptation of the short story, in which Miskatonic students spend a night in the Winthrop house and meet what is kept there
entries.why: A direct adaptation of a Lovecraft story, made outside any studio and on very little money, and one of the few films to put Randolph Carter on screen. Straight eighties slasher construction, though, with the creature revealed early and often, so the two judgements diverge.

entries.title: Necronomicon
entries.what: A three-part anthology from Christophe Gans, Shusuke Kaneko and Brian Yuzna, framed by Lovecraft himself breaking into a monastery library to copy the book
entries.why: An omnibus of three Lovecraft stories with the author written in as a character - the same fan-scholar impulse to treat the fiction as a set of documents. Executed as glossy nineties creature horror with heavy prosthetics - strong on grade, nil on tone.

entries.title: Cthulhu
entries.what: Daniel Gildark's Seattle-shot feature, loosely drawn from 'The Shadow over Innsmouth', in which a man returns to the Oregon coast town he escaped and finds his father leading a cult
entries.why: Released two years after the target, the other independent attempt of the decade to put the Cthulhu cult on film, and a useful contrast in strategy: it reaches for realism and contemporary drama where the target reaches for pastiche. Naturalistic digital colour, tone 0.

entries.title: Juha
entries.what: Aki Kaurismaki's silent black-and-white adaptation of the Finnish novel, with intertitles and a full score, about a farm couple broken up by a man in a convertible
entries.why: One of the very few modern features shot silent and monochrome on purpose, and the most austere of them - no winking, no nostalgia comedy, just the form used straight. Tones lower than it grades because the deadpan rural melodrama shares no dread with the target, only the grammar.

entries.title: Dr. Plonk
entries.what: Rolf de Heer's silent black-and-white comedy shot on a hand-cranked 1920s camera, about an inventor who builds a time machine to prove the world will end in 2008
entries.why: The most literal technical replication of silent-era production of any modern film - period camera, hand-cranked, undercranked - which is the same fidelity instinct as Mythoscope. Slapstick rather than dread, so the texture only half matches.

entries.title: Dracula: Pages from a Virgin's Diary
entries.what: Guy Maddin's film of the Royal Winnipeg Ballet's Dracula, told almost entirely without dialogue, with intertitles, irises, tinting and deliberately archaic camera tricks
entries.why: Modern silent-era pastiche used for horror rather than for comedy, with the same delight in obsolete optical devices - iris wipes, superimposition, stage fog - and the same willingness to let obvious artifice carry dread.

entries.title: Brand upon the Brain!
entries.what: Guy Maddin's black-and-white silent autobiography-as-melodrama about an island orphanage and a lighthouse, made with intertitles and scored for live performance
entries.why: Another film that chooses the silent idiom outright, and closer than most to the target's specific effects: hand-processed grain, intertitles doing the narration, a story delivered as feverish retrospective testimony.

entries.title: Tales from the Gimli Hospital
entries.what: Guy Maddin's first feature, made for almost nothing among friends in Winnipeg, a plague story staged in the deliberately degraded look of a lost 1920s film
entries.why: The clearest precedent for the whole idea: amateurs with no money making a feature that imitates a vanished era, and turning the shortfall - flat sound, grain, crude sets - into the point rather than the apology.

entries.title: Begotten
entries.what: E. Elias Merhige's wordless black-and-white feature, shot and then rephotographed frame by frame until the image is nearly abstract, in which a god disembowels himself and a figure is born from the remains
entries.why: Dialogue-free monochrome cosmic horror made over years by a tiny unpaid crew, where the creation myth stays at the edge of legibility and the extreme process is the horror. The withholding is total rather than tactical.

entries.title: Vampyr
entries.what: Carl Theodor Dreyer's near-silent vampire film, carried by intertitles and pages of an old book, with gauzed light, drifting shadows and a famous point-of-view burial
entries.why: Made at the hinge between silent and sound and built like a silent: almost no dialogue, the plot advanced by a book read on screen, and the horror produced by suggestion, misdirected shadow and things that are never explained. Very close to the target's method.

entries.title: The Phantom Carriage
entries.what: Victor Sjostrom's Swedish silent, in which a drunkard dies at midnight on New Year's Eve and must drive Death's cart, told in nested flashbacks with double-exposure ghosts
entries.why: Silent monochrome supernatural horror built on nested testimony and on one signature in-camera effect - the translucent cart - repeated until it becomes the film's whole atmosphere. The same economy of doing one impossible thing very well.

entries.title: The Golem: How He Came into the World
entries.what: Paul Wegener's silent prequel about a rabbi in 16th-century Prague who animates a clay figure, staged in Hans Poelzig's warped architectural sets
entries.why: Silent German horror with a hand-built creature and a conjuring sequence that is pure practical effect, plus the same interest in a summoned thing that is finally larger than the people who called it. Attribute match on period and mode.

entries.title: A Shoggoth on the Roof
entries.what: A 20-minute mockumentary written, produced and directed by Sean Branney and Andrew Leman, investigating a supposed 1979 attempt to stage Lovecraft as a Fiddler on the Roof musical; it premiered at the H.P. Lovecraft Film Festival in October 2000 but is indexed under 2001
entries.why: The only other HPLHS motion picture, by the same two men, and useful as evidence of the house sensibility - meticulous fabricated documents played entirely straight. A comic talking-heads short, so nothing of the target's texture survives. Marked short at 20 minutes.

entries.title: Caligula: The Ultimate Cut
entries.what: Thomas Negovan's 178-minute reconstruction of the 1979 Caligula, reassembled from the original camera negative and premiered at Cannes in 2023, with a newly recorded orchestral score
entries.why: Direct crew link: Troy Sterling Nies, the lead composer on The Call of Cthulhu and the sole composer on The Whisperer in Darkness, wrote the new score for this reconstruction. As a film it could not be further away - a vast, explicit, colour Roman epic - so this is the list's sharpest grade/tone split.

entries.title: King Kong
entries.what: Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack's film of a filmmaking expedition to an uncharted island, where Willis O'Brien's stop-motion ape is found behind a wall built by people who worship him
entries.why: Named by the HPLHS itself as one of the models for the sibling film The Whisperer in Darkness, and independently the direct descendant of The Lost World: monochrome, miniature-built, with a worshipped island monster reached by ship. Sound and full-blooded spectacle pull the tone away.

entries.title: In the Mouth of Madness
entries.what: John Carpenter's film about an insurance investigator sent to find a missing horror novelist whose books are rewriting reality, ending in a New England town that does not exist
entries.why: The most explicit Lovecraftian film not adapted from Lovecraft - the Old Ones, the forbidden text, the investigator who loses his mind assembling evidence - and the best-known example of the mode the target belongs to. Slick nineties studio horror that shows its monsters, so it grades far above what it tones.

entries.title: The Lighthouse
entries.what: Robert Eggers's black-and-white two-hander in 1.19:1, with two keepers on a New England rock, period diction, and a light neither we nor one of them is allowed to see
entries.why: Monochrome, boxy, period-obsessed maritime horror that withholds its central revelation until the last moment, from a director working the same seam of researched antiquarianism. Talks constantly and at length, though, where the target barely speaks.

entries.title: The Endless
entries.what: Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead's film - which they also wrote, shot, edited and starred in - about two brothers returning to the camp they escaped, where an unseen thing in the sky loops time
entries.why: The modern benchmark for cosmic horror kept almost entirely off screen, and made the same way the target was: a handful of friends doing every job themselves with no money, spending their one effect where it will land. Naturalistic sunlit digital video, so the texture does not carry over.

entries.title: Faust
entries.what: F. W. Murnau's last German film, a silent Faust staged with vast studio skies, models and a plague-bringing demon who spreads his wings over a town
entries.why: Silent monochrome supernatural spectacle built almost entirely out of miniatures, smoke and forced perspective - the same trick-work vocabulary, at the scale the target could only gesture at. Diverges the other way: only defensible as a connection, since nothing links the two beyond period kinship, but a viewer would recognise the texture at once.

entries.title: Waxworks
entries.what: Paul Leni's silent portmanteau, in which a poet hired to write stories for a fairground waxworks imagines three of them, each in its own distorted set
entries.why: Silent German horror organised as a frame plus assembled tales - the same anthology-of-testimony architecture - with sets that announce themselves as painted constructions. Diverges upward on tone: a loose connection, but the look is a direct match.

entries.title: The Hands of Orlac
entries.what: Robert Wiene's silent Austrian film about a pianist given a murderer's hands after a rail crash, played in enormous darkened voids
entries.why: From Caligari's director, and the purest example of silent horror that never shows you anything: the dread is entirely a man's conviction about something he cannot prove, held in empty black frames. Another case of a merely defensible link carrying a fully matching texture.

entries.title: The Phantom of the Opera
entries.what: Rupert Julian's silent Universal production, with Lon Chaney under the opera house, a self-designed makeup and a famous unmasking
entries.why: Silent monochrome horror built around a single withheld reveal and a hand-made monster effect, on the largest standing set of its era. The shape of the target's Cthulhu reveal, at studio scale - a generic period link, but the tone lands.

entries.title: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
entries.what: John S. Robertson's silent version with John Barrymore transforming largely through performance and in-camera tricks rather than makeup
entries.why: Silent-era horror from exactly the period the film reconstructs, and a demonstration of the same principle - that a transformation you half-see is worse than one you are shown. Grades low because the link is nothing but period and mode; tones high because that is exactly the register.

entries.title: The Man Who Laughs
entries.what: Paul Leni's late silent for Universal, with Conrad Veidt as a man whose face was carved into a permanent grin as a child
entries.why: Late-silent American horror with German craftsmen and a prosthetic that is the whole film, from the period the target imitates. More romance and melodrama than dread, so the texture only partly overlaps.

entries.title: The Unknown
entries.what: Tod Browning's silent circus melodrama with Lon Chaney as an armless knife-thrower who is not armless
entries.why: Silent American horror from the target's exact decade, built on physical deception and a reveal that is withheld to the end. A cruel melodrama rather than a supernatural one.

entries.title: Nosferatu the Vampyre
entries.what: Werner Herzog's colour remake of Murnau, with Klaus Kinski under the same makeup and long silences in place of plot
entries.why: A serious attempt to remake a silent film as itself rather than to modernise it - the same reverence for a 1920s original that the HPLHS acted on. Colour, sound and a glacial art-film pace put it in another register.

entries.title: Shadow of the Vampire
entries.what: E. Elias Merhige's film about the making of Nosferatu, imagining that Murnau hired a real vampire to play Orlok
entries.why: A whole feature about the craft and myth of 1920s horror production, with recreated silent footage - the same fascination with how those films were physically made. A talky colour period drama in the watching.

entries.title: Eraserhead
entries.what: David Lynch's black-and-white debut, shot over five years in scraps of time, about a man left with an unexplainable infant in an industrial city
entries.why: Monochrome horror made by a handful of people over years with no money and no explanations, where the one impossible creature is an in-house build nobody will discuss. The dread is sonic rather than visual, so only half the texture carries.

entries.title: Mad God
entries.what: Phil Tippett's almost wordless stop-motion feature, built intermittently over thirty years, in which a figure descends through strata of ruined industrial hell
entries.why: Frame-by-frame animation and miniature sets carrying an entire feature with no dialogue - the target's Cthulhu puppet taken to its limit by a career animator working on his own time. Colour, relentless and far more explicit.

entries.title: Equinox
entries.what: A stop-motion creature film begun by amateurs in their twenties and later re-cut for release, in which students find an ancient book in a canyon and are hunted by what it summons
entries.why: The clearest American precedent for the target's production mode: young enthusiasts making a monster feature at home with hand-animated creatures, an evil tome and forced-perspective compositing. Its patched-together colour has charm rather than dread.

entries.title: The Evil Dead
entries.what: Sam Raimi's debut, financed from friends and relatives and shot in a Tennessee cabin, in which a recording and a book of the dead wake something in the woods
entries.why: The canonical proof that a no-money horror feature made by friends can outlast studio product, and a first cousin in subject - the forbidden text that should not be read aloud. Frantic, gory and relentlessly shown.

entries.title: Raiders of the Lost Ark: The Adaptation
entries.what: A shot-for-shot fan remake of Raiders made by three Mississippi teenagers across seven summers, finished in 1989 and screened publicly from 2003
entries.why: The purest instance of fan filmmaking as a production mode - years of unpaid weekends, improvised effects, love substituting for budget - which is the tradition the HPLHS comes out of. Nothing of the target's texture.

entries.title: Star Wreck: In the Pirkinning
entries.what: A Finnish fan feature made over seven years by volunteers in their spare time, parodying Star Trek and Babylon 5, released free online the same year as The Call of Cthulhu
entries.why: The other 2005 landmark in what amateurs could finish and distribute themselves, and a direct comparison in economics: unpaid crew, home-built effects, an audience found outside the industry entirely. A broad digital comedy in the watching.

entries.title: The Blair Witch Project
entries.what: Daniel Myrick and Eduardo Sanchez's found-footage film, assembled as the recovered record of three student filmmakers lost in Maryland woods
entries.why: Horror built almost entirely from what is never shown, presented as recovered documents and testimony, made for almost nothing by people who had to invent their own techniques. Handheld video naturalism rather than composed monochrome.

entries.title: Skinamarink
entries.what: Kyle Edward Ball's micro-budget feature, shot in his parents' house, in which two children wake to find the doors and windows gone, filmed almost entirely as grainy corners and ceilings
entries.why: A no-money feature that makes its limitations the entire aesthetic - degraded image, nothing centred, the horror almost never on screen and never explained. The economy of the target, without any of its period craft.

entries.title: Enys Men
entries.what: Mark Jenkin's 16mm film about a volunteer on an uninhabited Cornish island recording a flower every day, cut to a rhythm that dissolves into repetition and apparition
entries.why: Hand-processed film grain, post-synced sound and an insistence on period texture used to build slow, unexplained dread on an island - a modern film that chooses obsolete technique as its subject matter, much as Mythoscope did. Colour and far slower.

entries.title: The Void
entries.what: Jeremy Gillespie and Steven Kostanski's siege film in an emptying hospital, with hooded figures outside and a doorway to somewhere else in the basement
entries.why: Lovecraft-inspired rather than adapted - no story of his is being filmed - and notable for practical creature effects crowdfunded and built by hand rather than rendered. Worth listing so the distinction between adaptation and homage stays visible.

entries.title: Annihilation
entries.what: Alex Garland's film of the VanderMeer novel, in which a survey team enters a shimmering zone where biology is being rewritten by something with no motive
entries.why: The most prominent modern expression of the target's actual idea - an indifferent force that is not evil and cannot be negotiated with - reached through a different literary line. A large, bright, effects-led studio film.

entries.title: A Field in England
entries.what: Wheatley's black-and-white Civil War picture: deserters press-ganged into digging in a single field eat mushrooms, and an alchemist's summoning takes hold
entries.why: A modern monochrome film that treats occult ritual as something which actually works, with a summoning at its centre and a landscape that turns hostile, which is the register the key already rewards in The Lighthouse and Enys Men. Wheatley shares the target's resourcefulness too, conjuring the supernatural out of actors, a field and a lens rather than money. Tone parts at the drug sequence and the graphic violence, which the HPLHS film's silent-era manners rule out.

entries.title: The Eyes of My Mother
entries.what: Pesce's debut: a surgeon's daughter, raised alone on a remote farm, keeps her mother's killer chained in the barn and acquires her later companions the same way
entries.why: The link is a genuine formal choice rather than a genre word: monochrome shot for depth and shadow, a short running time, and severe restraint about what is shown. The film holds a comparable hush. But nothing in it is cosmic, antiquarian or silent, and it is finally a naturalistic study of one damaged person, where the target's entire project is the pastiche of 1920s technique in the service of an indifferent universe. Defensible, no more.

entries.title: Hardware
entries.what: Richard Stanley's debut: a scavenged war-droid head reassembles itself in a Brutalist apartment and kills its way out, to Iggy Pop and Ministry
entries.why: No connection. A neon-lit industrial slasher with a rock soundtrack and a killer robot shares neither the target's subject, an intelligence to which mankind is beneath notice, nor its method, which is to reproduce the grammar of 1920s silent film shot by shot. Grimy practical effects is not a link: practical effects were the only kind either film could afford, decades apart and for unrelated reasons.

entries.title: The City of Lost Children
entries.what: Jeunet and Caro's designed dystopia, in which a strongman searches for his stolen brother in a port city where a scientist steals children's dreams
entries.why: Reaches this list on the word 'dreamlike'. Caro's design does descend distantly from the German expressionism the target imitates, but the film itself is a dense, brightly performed fantasy built around a rescue plot, and the target is a grave forty-seven-minute reconstruction of a silent horror picture. Nothing a viewer liked about either will be found in the other.

entries.title: Phase IV
entries.what: Saul Bass's only feature: two scientists sealed in an Arizona research dome are studied, outmanoeuvred and finally absorbed by an ant colony acting as one mind
entries.why: Cosmic indifference done straight, and done better than most films that set out to do it. The intelligence here regards the researchers roughly as Lovecraft's entities regard mankind, pursues purposes the film declines to translate, and ends by assimilating them in images it refuses to explain. The key reaches for Annihilation and The Endless on exactly this ground; Phase IV is the cleaner example and belongs above both. Its clinical daylight and macro photography sit a long way from the target's shadowed pastiche.

entries.title: November
entries.what: Rainer Sarnet's Estonian folk horror, shot in black-and-white: nineteenth-century villagers trade their souls to the Devil to animate kratts, servants assembled from farm implements
entries.why: Does in a modern film what the key rewards Haxan and The Phantom Carriage for: high-contrast monochrome, a pre-modern world in which the supernatural is simply part of the weather, and creatures built out of physical objects and filmed as though the camera had merely found them. The kratts are the same species of effect as the target's stop-motion Cthulhu, handmade and slightly wrong and better for it. November's black comedy and its love story are its own.

entries.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
entries.what: Tsukamoto's 16mm black-and-white body horror, in which a salaryman's flesh erupts into scrap metal, animated in stop-motion and pixilation
entries.why: Belongs on the same shelf as the key's Begotten and Eraserhead entries: black-and-white experimental horror about a body becoming something inhuman, made entirely outside an industry and dependent on stop-motion for its transformations. That is the whole of the defence. The target is a polite, faithful, carefully mannered reconstruction of silent-era storytelling, and Tetsuo has no manners, no period and no restraint.

entries.title: The Thing
entries.what: John Carpenter's Antarctic siege film: an organism thawed out of the ice assimilates and reproduces the men of an American research station one at a time
entries.why: Carpenter is already in the key through In the Mouth of Madness, which he describes as the third part of his Apocalypse Trilogy, preceded by The Thing, and whose title is taken from At the Mountains of Madness. The Thing is the trilogy's first term and the nearest Carpenter came to filming that novella: an Antarctic expedition, a thing recovered from the ice, and an organism whose purposes the film never converts into a motive. Tone diverges as far as it can — the target is a polite forty-seven-minute silent reconstruction in monochrome, and this is widescreen colour with a synthesiser pulse and the most graphic creature work of its decade.

entries.title: Event Horizon
entries.what: Paul W.S. Anderson's film: a rescue crew boards a starship that vanished through an artificial singularity seven years earlier and has returned from somewhere outside the universe
entries.why: Defensible on one idea, which the film does state clearly: a vessel has been somewhere for which human beings have no faculties, and what came back with it drives its witnesses to tear out their own eyes. Knowledge as the injury is the Lovecraftian proposition, and the key rewards it in The Endless and In the Mouth of Madness. The execution shares nothing with the target. Anderson's is a haunted-house picture of jump scares, strobed gore and an antagonist who explains himself at length in Latin, and the target's method is restraint, intertitles and an entity glimpsed in stop-motion for a few seconds.

entries.title: The Descent
entries.what: Neil Marshall's film: six women caving in an unmapped Appalachian system are hunted by a blind subterranean species
entries.why: A well-made survival horror about a predator, and a predator is precisely what cosmic horror is not. The crawlers are hungry, local and entirely comprehensible; the target's Cthulhu has no use for the men who wake it and is not hunting anybody. Claustrophobic tension and dark atmosphere are genre furniture shared with several hundred films, and the target is not even claustrophobic — its settings are an ocean, a Louisiana swamp and an attic full of papers.

entries.title: The Witch
entries.what: Robert Eggers's debut: a Puritan family exiled from their plantation in 1630 New England lose an infant to the woods, and the supernatural turns out to be exactly what they believe it to be
entries.why: Sits with the key's November and Häxan: a pre-modern world in which the supernatural is simply part of the weather, reconstructed with antiquarian care over period speech, fabric and light. Eggers's research method is a cousin of the HPLHS's, which rebuilt 1920s film grammar shot by shot. But The Witch's cosmology is Christian and personal — there is a devil, he wants your soul, and he negotiates for it — which is the opposite of an indifferent universe that has not noticed you exist. Grave, restrained and period enough to carry some of the target's manners.

entries.title: Under the Skin
entries.what: Jonathan Glazer's film, much of it shot with hidden cameras in Glasgow: a creature wearing a woman drives a van, collects men and delivers them into a black fluid beneath a derelict house
entries.why: Cosmic indifference done straight, which is the ground the previous pass rightly promoted Phase IV on. The film never translates its protagonist's purpose, never names her species, never supplies a plan, and treats human beings as material being processed — Lovecraft's proposition without a word of Lovecraft's vocabulary. It is also nearly wordless through its central passages and refuses to explain its ending, which the key rewards in Enys Men and Skinamarink. Glazer works in documentary-real modern Scotland where the target works in deliberate museum pastiche, but both hold the same hush and neither looks away.

entries.title: The Empty Man
entries.what: David Prior's debut: a retired detective investigating a missing girl in Missouri uncovers the Pontifex Institute, and learns that he is himself a tulpa, thought into existence by the cult
entries.why: The structural match nobody expects to find in a studio horror release. A man inherits an investigation, follows it into a cult that serves an entity older than the culture it surfaces in, and is destroyed by what the investigation reveals about his own place in it — which is the architecture of The Call of Cthulhu itself, Thurston's inherited papers and all. Wikipedia files it under Cthulhu Mythos films. Its Bhutan prologue is twenty minutes of cosmic dread with almost no dialogue. It is long, modern and has jump scares in it, which is what keeps the tone short of the target's silent-era composure.

entries.title: The Autopsy of Jane Doe
entries.what: André Øvredal's film: a father-and-son coroner team work through the night on an unidentified body whose intact exterior conceals catastrophic internal injuries
entries.why: Defensible on the engine rather than the cosmology. The film is a procedural in which each new fact recovered from the evidence makes the situation worse, until the investigators are destroyed by what they have learned — the shape of nearly every Lovecraft story, and of this one in particular. What stops it there is that the answer is fully supplied: a Salem witch trial, a human injustice, a curse with a motive and a target. The target's Cthulhu has no motive, and that difference is the whole of cosmic horror. Quiet, contained and severe enough to carry some of the manner.

entries.title: The Ritual
entries.what: David Bruckner's film: four English friends on a memorial hike in northern Sweden leave the trail and find a valley kept by a village that worships something antlered and faceless
entries.why: There is a genuine Lovecraftian object at the centre of it: an entity described as a bastard offspring of a god, ancient, anatomically wrong, and served by a human settlement that trades its neighbours for longevity. Remote geography, a degenerate worshipping community and a creature the design refuses to resolve are all things the target is made of. Against it, the film around that object is a lads-in-the-woods survival picture with a grief subplot, and the creature is finally fought and escaped, which the target's universe does not permit. Cold and restrained enough through the middle stretch to carry part of the register.

entries.title: Carnival of Souls
entries.what: Herk Harvey's only feature, made for around thirty thousand dollars by an industrial-film company in Lawrence, Kansas: a church organist who survives a car going off a bridge is drawn toward an abandoned lakeside pavilion by silent white-faced figures
entries.why: The best comparison in this pool for what the target actually is — a monochrome horror film made outside the industry by enthusiasts, conjuring everything it needs out of locations, lenses, an organ score and the good manners not to explain. Its figures are wordless, its dread is hollow rather than threatening, and its protagonist's real problem is that a larger arrangement decided about her before the film began, which is nearer Lovecraft's universe than most films that put his name in the credits. Sits naturally beside the key's Vampyr and The Phantom Carriage, and matches on hush, monochrome and gravity.

entries.title: Island of Lost Souls
entries.what: Erle C. Kenton's pre-Code adaptation of Wells, with Charles Laughton as Moreau and Bela Lugosi as the Sayer of the Law: a castaway finds an island where a vivisectionist has made a population of beast-men who chant a code in a stone hollow
entries.why: From the exact cinema the target is imitating — fog, expressionist shadow, minimal dialogue and late-silent visual grammar barely three years into sound — and banned in Britain for a quarter of a century on grounds of blasphemy, which is the charge Lovecraft's cults exist to attract. The House of Pain and the beast-men's chanted Law are the nearest thing on film to the target's swamp ritual: a degenerate community worshipping in a clearing, filmed as something the camera has intruded upon. Belongs with the key's King Kong, The Man Who Laughs and Waxworks, and is a better watch-next than at least two of them.

entries.title: Cabinet of Curiosities
entries.what: Guillermo del Toro's eight-part Netflix anthology, one hour per director and introduced by del Toro from a physical cabinet, of which two instalments are Lovecraft: 'Pickman's Model' from the 1919 story and 'Dreams in the Witch House' from 1933
entries.why: The strongest claim recent television has on this target. It is a portmanteau that actually adapts Lovecraft rather than borrowing his adjectives, made in an avowedly Gothic and Grand Guignol house style, and the key already holds Necronomicon at this grade for doing the same job in 1993. Everything about the watching is the other way round: lavish colour, a score, dialogue throughout, prosthetic horror delivered in full, and an hour per story in which to explain itself, against forty-seven wordless minutes that spend their entire effects budget on one withheld stop-motion reveal. Grades well above its tone.

entries.title: Hagazussa
entries.what: Lukas Feigelfeld's Austrian-German debut: a goatherd in the fifteenth-century Alps, shunned by her village after her mother's death, is driven through isolation, assault and mushrooms into drowning her own child and dying alone on a mountainside, told with almost no dialogue over a dark-ambient score by MMMD
entries.why: The folk-horror label on its own would earn a zero here, and nearly does. What saves it is a real formal property rather than a genre word: it is close to wordless, it refuses to explain, and it lets dread accumulate for long stretches with nothing but a picture and a drone to carry it, which is the discipline the target works under by necessity. The connection stops there. Hagazussa is colour, it is a naturalistic study of one woman's degradation with the supernatural left optional, and it has no interest whatever in film technique as subject matter, where the target's whole project is rebuilding 1920s silent grammar shot by shot. A shared taste for slowness is not a lineage. Defensible on register, no more.

entries.title: Archive 81
entries.what: Netflix's eight-episode series from the 2016 podcast, cancelled after one season: a video conservator restores deteriorating Hi8 tapes shot by a graduate student in 1994, whose documentary on an apartment building leads to the Baldung coven and Kaelego, a thing the series calls both god and demon, with the roots of it reaching back to 1924
entries.why: The architecture is the target's own, and nothing else on this list can say that. A man inherits a dead stranger's records, assembles from them a coherent account of a cult devoted to an entity older than anyone left alive, and is destroyed by the place that account turns out to give him in it - which is Thurston with his great-uncle's papers, down to the nested layers of testimony and material dated to the 1920s. The key rates The Empty Man at this grade on exactly that structural claim. It is the opposite end of the medium to sit through: eight hours of glossy digital colour with a romance, cliffhangers, jump scares and a mythology narrated aloud as it goes. The 1994 tape material is the only texture the two share, and it is a fraction of the running time. Grades on its shape, tones nothing like it.

entries.title: The Head Hunter
entries.what: Jordan Downey's seventy-two-minute film, made for thirty thousand dollars in Portugal, Norway and California: a lone medieval bounty hunter keeps his kills' heads nailed to the wall of his hut, waiting for the creature that took his daughter. The script ran forty pages and has barely a line of dialogue in it, and the heads were built out of clearance Halloween masks stained and sealed under melted plastic
entries.why: The closest thing here to the target's method rather than its subject. A feature-length horror film with no money, effectively one actor and almost no speech, which converts its poverty into a style: long silences, a monster kept off screen until the last reel, and creature work visibly hand-made from whatever was going cheap. That is what Mythoscope was - a constraint dressed up as a choice - and the key rewards Die Farbe and Skinamarink for the same economy. It parts from the target on everything else: muddy digital colour, sound design doing the work the target had to do with pictures alone, and a final act that hands over the gore a silent-era pastiche would never show.

entries.title: Errementari: The Blacksmith and the Devil
entries.what: Paul Urkijo Alijo's first feature, in Alavese Basque: in Araba in 1843, in the wake of the First Carlist War, a blacksmith keeps a demon chained in his forge and an orphan girl lets it out. Taken from the Basque telling of the Smith and the Devil collected by Joxemiel Barandiaran
entries.why: Arrives on 'folklore-driven horror with an antique texture', which describes several hundred films, and nothing survives contact with the target. Errementari is a colour period fable with a score, continuous dialogue, a rescue plot, an expedition to Hell and a devil who bargains, loses and can be outwitted - which is the exact inverse of an intelligence to which mankind is beneath notice. The key does admit modern folk horror, but on specific grounds it can name: November for its monochrome and its creatures assembled out of farm tools, The Witch for a research method that is a genuine cousin of the HPLHS's shot-by-shot reconstruction. Errementari offers neither, and a viewer who came out of the target wanting more of what it was doing would find none of it here.

entries.title: Picnic at Hanging Rock
entries.what: Peter Weir's Australian film: on Valentine's Day 1900 three schoolgirls and a teacher walk up a volcanic outcrop in Victoria and are never found, shot through bridal veil stretched over the lens and scored to Gheorghe Zamfir's pan flute
entries.why: One real point of contact and it is a good one - an inquiry that yields nothing, a disappearance the film flatly declines to explain, and an old landscape that is indifferent to the Europeans standing on it and will not account for itself. That is nearer Lovecraft's actual proposition than most of the films that carry his name. Against it, and it is decisive: the target is not an unexplained film at all. Thurston's papers assemble a complete account, name the cult, date the events and finally show you the thing; its horror is in what the explanation means, not in its absence. And where the target is high-contrast monochrome composed for dread, Weir's is a warm, diffused, unhurried reverie. Defensible.
